In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the effects of the treatment of the brain on the brain's behavior.
the effects of the drug reserpine on the uptake of amine by the amine granule of sympathetic nerves.
the study of the effects of reserpine on the monoamine storage mechanism and the recovery of the mechanism in the central and peripheral nervous systems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the reserpine treatment of the transected animals resulted in a more pronounced decrease of the monoamine uptake-storage mechanism than in the intact animals.

the reserpine effect on the monoamine uptake-storage mechanism is not due to a permanent damage to the granule structure, but to the disappearance of a very highly bound fraction of reserpine from them.
the amine uptake mechanism recovers in the nerve granules of reserpinized animals at the time of the functional recovery, but not in the granules in the cell bodies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the uptake mechanism in the amine granule membrane is recovered before the monoamine levels.

the amine uptake-storage mechanism in the nerve granules recovers in the central nervous systems of reserpinized rats after transection of the axons, but only after a long delay in the peripheral nerves.
axotomy does not influence the recovery of the uptake-storage mechanism in the central monoamine neurons.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the use of the amine storage and uptake mechanisms in the nerve terminals is not a prerequisite for nerve function, but is rather a mechanism which can be turned on or off by the central nervous system, depending on its needs.
there is a very strong correlation between the ability of the granules to take in amine and the nerve function.
the brain can recover from the effects of a drug that blocks its ability to store dopamine and other neurotransmitters, and that the process of recovery is very fast.
